steps.premise: Donors arriving while the hall is closed may leave boxes in the corridor.
steps.action: Publicize staffed drop-off hours and the place to bring donations.
steps.consequence: Donors can hand puzzles to someone instead of leaving them in the corridor.
steps.quote: When the hall is closed, people who came specifically to donate a puzzle may leave their boxes in a corridor. Advertise the hours when someone will be on hand to accept puzzles, and say where to bring them during those hours.

steps.premise: Similar boxes from the same brand can contain different numbers of pieces.
steps.action: Copy the manufacturer's title and stated piece count onto a label for each donation.
steps.consequence: Browsers can compare the likely work involved in assembling the puzzles.
steps.quote: A familiar brand may use the same box design for puzzles with different piece counts. For each donated puzzle, copy the title and stated piece count from the manufacturer's panel onto a label so people can compare how much work each puzzle might take.

steps.premise: Even with the same piece count, the image can affect how difficult a puzzle feels.
steps.action: Invite contributors to describe the image in plain language and identify parts they found difficult.
steps.consequence: Takers can judge what kind of challenge the image presents.
steps.quote: Assembling a thousand pieces that show distinct illustrated characters feels different from assembling a thousand pieces of sky. Let contributors describe the image in plain language and mention which parts they found challenging to assemble.

steps.premise: People differ in how much they mind a missing piece.
steps.action: Group playable incomplete puzzles together and mark the known gap with a removable note on the box picture.
steps.consequence: Takers can see what is missing and decide whether to take the puzzle.
steps.quote: A missing piece bothers some people more than others. Group playable incomplete puzzles together and mark the known gap on the box picture with a removable note so takers can decide for themselves.

steps.premise: A box may open when someone tilts it to get it out of a tight stack.
steps.action: Have intake volunteers bag loose pieces in a resealable bag and seal it before shelving the box.
steps.consequence: The pieces stay together if the box opens.
steps.quote: Tilting a box to pull it from a tight stack can cause it to open. Ask intake volunteers to put loose pieces in a resealable bag and seal it before shelving the box.

steps.premise: Someone with limited grip may find small, closely packed pieces hard to handle.
steps.action: Mark large-piece sets with the actual piece size and show a sample outline on their cards.
steps.consequence: Browsers can compare piece sizes and judge which they could handle.
steps.quote: Small, tightly packed pieces can be awkward for someone with limited grip to handle. Mark large-piece sets with their actual piece size and keep a sample outline on their cards for comparison.

steps.premise: A small child may reach the bottom shelf while their caregiver browses.
steps.action: Use that shelf only for boxed children's puzzles and keep each box's original age guidance visible.
steps.consequence: Children encounter children's sets within reach, and caregivers can check the intended age.
steps.quote: While a caregiver browses, a small child may be able to reach anything on the bottom shelf. Reserve that shelf for boxed children's puzzles, with the original age guidance visible on each box.

steps.premise: A builder may rely entirely on the picture on the lid.
steps.action: Check that the lid image is legible and include a clean image from the donor when a damaged lid needs a replacement reference.
steps.consequence: The builder has a usable picture to consult during assembly.
steps.quote: The picture on the lid may be the only reference someone has while assembling the puzzle. Check that it's legible and include a clean image from the donor if a damaged lid needs a substitute.

steps.premise: Damp cardboard can spoil nearby boxes in the closed cupboard.
steps.action: Inspect donations in good light and ask donors to take back boxes showing moisture or mildew.
steps.consequence: Damp boxes stay out of the cupboard, protecting neighboring puzzles.
steps.quote: Once the cupboard is closed, damp cardboard can spoil the boxes next to it. Inspect incoming boxes in good light and ask the donor to take back any that show signs of moisture or mildew.

steps.premise: Someone who discovers a problem at home may have forgotten the puzzle title.
steps.action: Give every accepted box a short identifier.
steps.consequence: Residents can report the affected puzzle without having to describe its artwork.
steps.quote: By the time someone notices a problem at home, they may have forgotten the puzzle's title. Give each accepted box a short identifier so a resident can report a problem without having to describe the artwork.

steps.premise: A piece thought missing can turn up later.
steps.action: Keep found pieces behind the desk in labeled envelopes and match them by puzzle identifier.
steps.consequence: A recovered piece can rejoin its puzzle and make it complete again.
steps.quote: A piece reported missing may turn up under the dining table and make the puzzle complete again. Keep found pieces in labeled envelopes behind the desk and use the puzzle identifier to match them.

steps.premise: Some neighbors want to see the finished puzzle before choosing it.
steps.action: Invite builders to share a snapshot for the noticeboard and display the box identifier beneath it.
steps.consequence: A neighbor who likes the finished picture can find that particular puzzle.
steps.quote: Sometimes neighbors need to see what a finished puzzle looks like before choosing it. Invite builders to share a snapshot for a noticeboard and put the box identifier beneath the photo so someone can look for that same puzzle.
